title: A Governor Murdered at Dinner
overview: After Babylon destroys Jerusalem, a member of the old royal family murders the governor Babylon appointed and kills many others, leaving the survivors so afraid of reprisal that they head for Egypt.

parts.label: Murder at the meal (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Gedaliah was the governor Babylon set over ruined Judah, and Ishmael, from the old royal family, killed him while they shared a meal, a setting that normally signaled trust. Ishmael also killed the people of Judah with Gedaliah and the Babylonian soldiers there, possibly resenting a ruler outside the royal line, and Johanan had earlier warned that the king of Ammon sent him.

parts.label: Mourning pilgrims killed (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Eighty men from northern towns came in mourning, with shaved beards, torn clothes and cut skin, bringing grain and incense to the site of the ruined temple in Jerusalem. Ishmael went out weeping to meet them, which many readers take as a show of false grief, then killed all but ten, who saved themselves by offering food stores hidden in a field.

parts.label: An old cistern becomes a grave (v. 9)
parts.note: The bodies were thrown into a large water cistern that King Asa had built long before when he fortified Mizpah against the northern kingdom of Israel. Something made to help the town survive a siege became a mass grave.

parts.label: Survivors taken captive (v. 10)
parts.note: Ishmael marched the rest of Mizpah's people, including the king's daughters, toward Ammon, the neighboring kingdom east of the Jordan River. Jeremiah had been living at Mizpah, so he was likely among them.

parts.label: Johanan's rescue (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: Johanan, an army officer who had warned Gedaliah about Ishmael, caught up with him at the large pool in Gibeon. The captives gladly went over to Johanan, but Ishmael escaped to Ammon with eight men.

parts.label: Fear drives them south (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: The rescued group stopped near Bethlehem at a place called Geruth Kimham, on their way to Egypt. They feared Babylon would punish them all for the murder of its governor, which sets up the next chapter.

think: After a disaster, what makes some people turn on their own community instead of helping it rebuild?
